batik-tulis-parang-barong.name: Parang Barong Batik
batik-tulis-parang-barong.tagline: Ranks of diagonal blade forms on deep indigo, parted by dotted gold bands.
batik-tulis-parang-barong.description: Parang is among the best known motifs of the Javanese courts: a repeating curved form set on a 45-degree diagonal, separated by a dotted band called mlinjon. The barong version uses the largest scale in the parang family, so the motif still reads clearly even on a short cut. Printed on fine 130 gsm cotton with a dense indigo ground and motif lines in raw-cotton cream.
batik-tulis-parang-barong.story: In the dress conventions of the Surakarta court, parang was once among the motifs whose use was governed by the wearer's standing, and barong was the largest of its sizes. Those rules no longer bind, but the diagonal arrangement is still chosen for the simple reason that it makes the wearer look taller.
bestFor: Large decorative panels and cushion covers
care: Hand wash in cold water with lerak soap or a bleach-free detergent
Do not soak for more than 15 minutes, or the indigo may bleed into the light areas
Dry inside out in the shade, away from direct sun
Iron on a medium setting from the reverse side

tenun-ikat-sumba-tanah.name: Sumba Ikat, Earth
tenun-ikat-sumba-tanah.tagline: Rows of arrowheads with softly feathered edges in earth red and ivory.
tenun-ikat-sumba-tanah.description: The signature of ikat is in the edges: the threads are bound and dyed before weaving, so the motif outline is never as sharp as a print. Elongated diamonds are set in rows between horizontal bands. At 210 gsm this cotton is substantial enough to hold its shape while still sewing well on a domestic machine.
tenun-ikat-sumba-tanah.story: East Sumba is known for ikat in earth tones drawn from root and bark dyes. Binding the threads before dyeing demands that the whole design be worked out at the very start, while the yarn is still stretched loose on the frame.
bestFor: Outer layers, waistcoats, and light jackets
care: Hand wash separately for the first wash, as colour may run
Use cold water and never scrub the patterned surface
Dry flat so the weave does not stretch out of shape
Iron with a pressing cloth over the fabric

songket-palembang-lepus.name: Palembang Songket Lepus
songket-palembang-lepus.tagline: A lattice of gold thread covering almost the whole surface of ruby silk.
songket-palembang-lepus.description: Lepus is the songket variant in which the gold thread covers nearly the entire field rather than just the borders. Stacked diamonds carry a centre point with small crosses between them. Woven on a silk ground with metallic thread, producing a 260 gsm cloth that is heavy, lustrous, and falls in decisive folds.
songket-palembang-lepus.story: Songket from Palembang is traditionally made by laying a supplementary thread into every row of the weave — slow work, and the reason this kind of cloth has always carried a higher price than plain weaving. This is one of the heaviest fabrics in our catalogue.
care: Dry cleaning is strongly recommended
Never wring or twist, as this snaps the metallic thread
Store rolled rather than folded, so the gold does not break along fold lines
Iron on low from the reverse side with a pressing cloth

batik-mega-mendung-cirebon.name: Mega Mendung Batik
batik-mega-mendung-cirebon.tagline: Tiered rolling clouds shifting from deep sea blue to open sky.
batik-mega-mendung-cirebon.description: Mega mendung is built from stacked cloud curves in several gradations of colour — seven tiers by tradition. This version uses four tiers of blue on a light 125 gsm cotton, the sort of cloth that is most comfortable in heat and the most forgiving to sew.
batik-mega-mendung-cirebon.story: This cloud motif from Cirebon emerged where the north coast of Java met Chinese traders, visible in the scrolling cloud form common in Chinese art but given the tiered colour arrangement characteristic of the Javanese coast.
care: Machine washable on a gentle cycle inside a laundry bag
Use cold water and a bleach-free detergent
Dry in the shade so the blue gradation does not fade
Iron on medium while the cloth is still slightly damp

lurik-yogya-klasik.name: Classic Yogya Lurik
lurik-yogya-klasik.tagline: Warp stripes of varying width in cream, dark brown, and brick.
lurik-yogya-klasik.description: Lurik is made from vertical stripes whose widths are counted out one by one as the warp is dressed. Nothing is printed — the entire pattern comes from the order of the coloured threads. A 210 gsm cotton at 90 cm wide, which is the characteristic width of a non-mechanical loom.
lurik-yogya-klasik.story: Lurik was once everyday working cloth in Central Java, worn precisely because it was plain and hard-wearing. Each stripe arrangement carries a name taken from ordinary things, such as telu-pat for a sequence of three and four.
bestFor: Aprons, cushion covers, and table linen
care: Machine wash cold on a normal cycle
Wash before cutting, as handwoven cotton shrinks 3–5%
Tumble drying on low is acceptable
Iron on medium, following the direction of the stripes

ulos-batak-ragidup.name: Ragidup Ulos
ulos-batak-ragidup.tagline: Alternating red and cream bands with triangular end panels on black.
ulos-batak-ragidup.description: An ulos is read through its horizontal bands: wide dark fields interrupted by fine red and gold lines, closed at both ends by panels of triangular motifs. A 230 gsm cotton with a dense weave, so the cloth feels solid and is not at all sheer.
ulos-batak-ragidup.story: Ragidup is among the more intricate ulos arrangements, because its end panels are woven separately and then joined. In Batak Toba custom, ulos have a role in various life ceremonies, and the type given is matched to the occasion.
care: Hand wash in cold water and do not soak for long
Keep away from light-coloured items on the first wash
Dry flat in the shade
Iron with a pressing cloth, avoiding the fringes

tenun-endek-bali-giri.name: Bali Endek Giri
tenun-endek-bali-giri.tagline: Rows of gold lozenges set close together on an emerald ground.
tenun-endek-bali-giri.description: Endek applies the ikat technique to the weft threads only, which keeps the motif small and tightly spaced compared to double ikat. Lozenges sit in an even grid with terracotta accents between them. A cotton and rayon blend at 160 gsm, which drapes softly while still holding a pressed fold.
tenun-endek-bali-giri.story: Endek is worn widely in Bali for temple dress and uniforms alike, and in 2021 the provincial government encouraged its use through a circular on wearing endek on set days. As a result, endek motifs are now produced in a much wider range of colours.
care: Hand wash, or machine wash cold on a gentle cycle
Avoid bleach and acidic fabric softeners
Dry inside out in the shade
Iron on low, as rayon is sensitive to heat

sasirangan-banjar-gelombang.name: Sasirangan Gelombang
sasirangan-banjar-gelombang.tagline: Ripples of stitch resist in magenta, purple, and turmeric yellow.
sasirangan-banjar-gelombang.description: Sasirangan is made by running a basting stitch along a drawn pattern, pulling the thread tight, and then dyeing — the gathered areas resist the colour and leave a wavy line behind. Because the tension is never quite the same twice, each length has a slightly different ripple. Cotton at 140 gsm.
sasirangan-banjar-gelombang.story: The name sasirangan comes from menyirang, meaning to baste. The cloth comes from South Kalimantan and was traditionally made in small quantities to order, since every pattern has to be basted again from scratch.
care: Hand wash separately for the first three washes
Use cold water and a mild, bleach-free soap
Do not scrub the rippled areas
Iron on medium from the reverse side

batik-kawung-solo-sogan.name: Kawung Sogan Batik
batik-kawung-solo-sogan.tagline: Four interlocking ellipses forming a tight grid in sogan brown.
batik-kawung-solo-sogan.description: Kawung is built from four ellipses interlocking around a central point, repeating into a grid. Because the pattern is small and regular, kawung is among the easiest motifs to combine with other things. Dyed in sogan tones — the yellow-brown traditionally drawn from soga bark. Cotton at 128 gsm.
batik-kawung-solo-sogan.story: Kawung is one of the oldest recorded motifs in Java and is often linked to the cross-section of a sugar palm fruit. Its thoroughly regular arrangement means it has frequently served as a ground pattern beneath other ornament.
care: Machine wash cold on a gentle cycle
Avoid bleach, which turns the sogan brown reddish
Dry in the shade
Iron on medium while the cloth is still damp

tapis-lampung-pucuk-rebung.name: Lampung Tapis Pucuk Rebung
tapis-lampung-pucuk-rebung.tagline: Bands of gold thread and rows of bamboo-shoot triangles on midnight blue.
tapis-lampung-pucuk-rebung.description: Tapis is arranged as a sequence of horizontal bands: close-set gold lines, a row of pucuk rebung triangles, and undulating bands between them. Metallic thread is couched onto a woven cotton ground, producing a 275 gsm cloth — the second heaviest in this catalogue.
tapis-lampung-pucuk-rebung.story: Pucuk rebung — the triangle that echoes a young bamboo shoot — is among the most widespread ornaments in Sumatran cloth, from Lampung tapis to Minangkabau songket. The row of triangles is usually placed along the cloth's border.
care: Dry clean only
Store rolled with acid-free paper between the layers
Never iron directly over the gold thread
Keep out of damp storage, or the metallic thread will tarnish

lipa-sabbe-bugis-sengkang.name: Lipa' Sabbe Sengkang
lipa-sabbe-bugis-sengkang.tagline: Ruby silk checks cut through by lines of gold and deep green.
lipa-sabbe-bugis-sengkang.description: Lipa' sabbe means silk sarong in Bugis. The motif is a large check formed by the difference between the warp and weft colours, then cut through with fine contrasting lines. Silk at 120 gsm — the lightest cloth in this catalogue, with a sheen that shifts as the light moves.
lipa-sabbe-bugis-sengkang.story: Sengkang, in Wajo Regency of South Sulawesi, is known as a centre of silk weaving, including the rearing of the silkworms themselves. The size of the check on a lipa' sabbe traditionally distinguished its wearer, though the choice is freer today.
care: Dry clean, or hand wash very carefully with baby shampoo
Never wring — press gently between towels
Dry flat in the shade, away from direct light
Iron on the lowest setting from the reverse side

tenun-troso-jepara-ombak.name: Troso Ombak
tenun-troso-jepara-ombak.tagline: Copper and sea-green zigzags moving like ripples across water.
tenun-troso-jepara-ombak.description: The zigzag in Troso weaving is formed by ordering the weft threads so the line rises and falls at a regular interval. The copper accent gives a warm contrast against the sea-green ground. A cotton and rayon blend at 175 gsm, light enough for clothing while still reading as textured.
tenun-troso-jepara-ombak.story: The village of Troso in Jepara built weaving into its main craft and became known for taking commissioned motifs. Because of that, the range of patterns coming out of Troso is far wider than at centres that keep to a single canon.
bestFor: Light outer layers and casual shirts
care: Hand wash in cold water with a mild soap
Do not soak together with light-coloured fabrics
Dry flat so the weave does not pull to one side
Iron on low, as the cloth contains rayon
